description: MMMU is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks requiring college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering, spanning 30 subjects and 183 subfields with 30 heterogeneous image types. The ziyjiang_MMEB_Test_Instruct variant is an instruction-formatted version of the MMMU test split for use in multimodal embedding benchmarking.
name: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark) - Test Instruct variant
publisher: IN.AI Research, University of Waterloo, The Ohio State University
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, specializing in the relevant majors covered by the benchmark. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected (3 per subject) to represent experts in the corresponding 30 subjects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled error cases from GPT-4V predictions, analyzed by expert annotators who identified root causes. Distribution: 35% perceptual errors, 29% lack of knowledge, 26% reasoning errors, 4% textual understanding errors, 3% rejection to answer, 2% annotation errors, 1% answer extraction errors. Human expert performance ranged from 76.2% (worst) to 88.6% (best) on the validation set.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web interface developed for data annotation and verification
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators (university students specializing in relevant majors) collected questions from textbooks and online resources. They were instructed to: (1) adhere to copyright and licensing regulations; (2) select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination; (3) annotate all fields including question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation. A secondary review team vetted annotations for quality. Questions were categorized into difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded.
rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination concerns. The benchmark excludes subjects like law and linguistics where it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were manually collected by over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in various majors. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks, online resources, and created new questions based on their expertise. The collection process involved three stages: selecting subjects, recruiting annotators, and collecting questions while adhering to copyright and license regulations.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources. The initial collection resulted in approximately 13K questions from various sources before quality filtering.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Some subjects like law and linguistics were excluded due to difficulty finding enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two-step data cleaning: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications; (2) problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. Finally, problems were categorized into four difficulty levels, and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, which is defined as AI systems reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks. Such systems could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark helps the community assess and track this progress responsibly.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal foundation models on expert-level perception and reasoning tasks requiring college-level domain knowledge. Benchmarking progress towards Expert AGI. Assessing LMMs' capabilities in perception, knowledge recall, and reasoning across diverse academic disciplines.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotators were instructed to avoid collecting questions that contain any private information. Data privacy compliance with privacy laws and ethical standards in data handling is paramount.

evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotators are instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given the arising data contamination concerns of foundation models, the annotators are advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Tianyu Zheng developed a user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification. The interface design significantly improved the workflow for data curation.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking. This step requires authors to ensure adherence to a standardized format, undertaking necessary corrections where deviations are found. evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We meticulously examine 150 randomly sampled error instances from GPT-4V's predictions. These instances are analyzed by expert annotators who identify the root causes of mispredictions based on their knowledge and the golden explanations if available.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: MMMU , like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition [57], because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We believe MMMU will stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Level 3, or Expert AGI, marks a critical milestone. It denotes an AI system that reaches "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve "the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor" for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Data Privacy: Compliance with privacy laws and ethical standards in data handling is paramount. The annotators should avoid collecting questions that contain any private information.
